tier_reason: The README (the benchmark_url) states first-party averaged results versus std::stack over std::deque (82%, 83%, 80%, 82% and 724% faster for 1-, 4-, 8-, 40- and 490-byte types) with no compiler, flags, CPU or benchmark code; the full benchmark page plflib.org/stack.htm returned EGRESS_BLOCKED and no mattreecebentley GitHub repository carries the benchmark harness, so the result cannot be checked beyond first-party numbers.

corrections.caveats: First-party numbers taken from the README only. The full benchmark page (plflib.org/stack.htm#benchmarks) is blocked by this environment's egress policy, so compiler, flags, CPU, OS and the per-size graphs could not be checked, and the README gives only averages. The repo holds plf_stack.h, plf_tools.h and plf_stack_test_suite.cpp (functional tests with no timing code); none of the author's GitHub repositories carries the benchmark harness, so the numbers cannot be reproduced from GitHub. Baseline is std::deque-backed std::stack only; the README's 'faster than all std:: containers in a stack context' for vector and list comes with no numbers on the page I could open. The 724% figure is for 490-byte elements, where the README itself says libstdc++'s deque degenerates into a linked list because of its 512-byte block limit, so that row reflects a libstdc++ weakness rather than a general result. Libc++ and MSVC STL results are not given in the README (a search snippet says the site also links MSVC graphs; not verified).

notes: README numbers match the record exactly; metadata confirmed on github.com (79 stars, 7 forks, Zlib, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-03 'Add files via upload', so active). Tier stays C until someone with access to plflib.org/stack.htm checks compiler, flags, CPU and whether the benchmark code is downloadable there (the sibling plf_list and plf_bitsets entries reached A from plflib.org pages).

tier_reason: Independent community shootout (NoAvailableAlias/signal-slot-benchmarks, run by the nano-signal-slot author, not SimpleSignal's) with public harness code (benchmark.hpp, benchmark/hpp/benchmark_lss.hpp, vendored lib/larspensjo/SimpleSignal) showing SimpleSignal ahead of Boost Signals2 st and libsigc++; only 'Visual Studio 19 x64 release' is stated and flags and CPU are not, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: MSVC thread-unsafe table: emission 137,345 vs Boost Signals2 st 44,228 (3.1x) and libsigcplusplus 72,139 (1.9x); score 170,724 vs 62,979 (2.7x) and 80,450 (2.1x); connect 9,994 vs 3,655 (2.7x) vs Boost Signals2 st; construction 4,897 vs 286 (17x) and destruction 6,766 vs 592 (11x) vs Boost Signals2 st, but those two columns are excluded from the score. Ratios derived from page data. Higher is better (samples per unit time over sizes [2, 64]).
corrections.caveats: Ranks 15th of 24 libraries by score in the thread-unsafe table; jeffomatic jl_signal (415,278), vdksoft signals st (309,575), Nuclex Events (215,607) and nano-signal-slot st (196,413) all score higher. Its emission figure (137,345) is the highest in the column but within 1% of eight other libraries (mwthinker Signal 137,227, jl_signal 136,499, Wink-Signals 136,024, Nuclex 135,934), so emission is at a shared ceiling and the large ratios are against Boost.Signals2 and libsigc++ rather than against other lightweight signals. Construction and destruction are marked 'excluded from scoring'; the score is the sum of connect, disconnect, reconnect, emit, all and threaded (threaded is 0 for every thread-unsafe library). Windows MSVC results only (refreshed May-June 2020 per the suite's commits); the GCC page is marked 'HELP NEEDED' and has no SimpleSignal row. CPU, compiler flags and Boost version are not stated, and the suite's own foreword says the benchmarks do not depict real-world usage. The suite's metadata row lists SimpleSignal's data structure as std::vector, but the library (and the vendored copy, identical to upstream except a const on size()) stores a std::list of std::shared_ptr<std::function>. The original Simple::Signal comparison (Tim Janik's testbit.eu post, referenced from the README) was not opened; the repo's own test.cpp times only Simple::Signal against a plain callback loop and publishes no numbers. Repo last updated 2019-07-24. CC0-1.0 dedication: no patent grant. The seed's guessed category (serialization-json) was wrong; this is a signal/slot (observer callback) library.

notes: All numbers match the SimpleSignal, Boost Signals2 st and libsigcplusplus rows on the MSVC results page; metadata confirmed (179 stars, 42 forks, CC0-1.0, not a fork, 26 commits, last commit 2019-07-24, so abandoned). No spec category fits exactly: signals-and-callbacks is off-spec; the closest Wave 1 category is smart-pointers-and-refcount (its std::function row, where delegate, sy_callback.hpp, SmallFunction and woid are filed), though SimpleSignal's baseline is Boost.Signals2/libsigc++ rather than std::function, so keep baseline_in_list false and consider a category override to smart-pointers-and-refcount with that shortcoming recorded.

tier_reason: First-party README table from the repo's demo.c (public code) against libc qsort, but compiler, flags and CPU model for the run are unstated (only '2014-era MacBook Pro'), so it is first-party with partial methodology.

corrections.claimed_speedup: demo.c output on a 2014-era MacBook Pro, 10,000 int64_t: quick sort 579 us vs stdlib qsort 1285 us (about 2.2x, derived from page data); heap sort 592, in-place merge sort 903, merge sort 999, tim sort 1005, shell sort 1054, sqrt sort 1095 and grail sort 1220 us are also below qsort's 1285 us; binary insertion (13,443 us) and selection sort (127,176 us) are far slower; stdlib mergesort 1299 us and heapsort 2109 us are slower than qsort.
corrections.caveats: The README table comes from one run (RUNS is 1 in demo.c, timed with gettimeofday at microsecond resolution) of one 10,000-element lrand48 array on an unnamed 2014 laptop, with compiler and flags unstated. The baseline is C qsort calling through a function pointer (and, since the stdlib heapsort and mergesort rows are compiled only on non-Linux, non-Cygwin platforms, macOS/BSD libc qsort), not std::sort or an inlined-comparator sort, so the gap measures comparator inlining more than algorithm quality; qsort is also not in the sorting category's baseline list. The demo uses the subtraction comparator (x - y), safe here only because lrand48 values are non-negative. The table predates later code changes (gallop revert 2020, binary-insertion small sorts 2021, grail and sqrt sort moved to sort_extra.h in 2024), so it reflects older code. Only quick sort, heap sort and in-place merge sort show a clear win; the README itself says results depend on the machine and data. benchmark.c in the repo (100,000 elements, timed loops) is more careful but no results from it are published.

notes: README numbers match the record; metadata confirmed on github.com (476 stars, 88 forks, MIT, not a fork, last commit 2024-02-13 'Add GitHub Actions (#88)', so stale). Baseline is C qsort rather than a listed std:: facility, so baseline_in_list is corrected to false.
